summary_student.text: Gas mixtures of hydrogen, methane or ethylene were fed through a small ball-shaped porous burner aboard the International Space Station to make round flames. The team measured how these flames grow, flicker and go out, and compared the results with computer simulations. Knowing the limits where flames go out helps predict how fires behave in weightlessness.

summary_professional.text: Spherical diffusion flames were stabilized on a spherical porous burner in ACME in the Combustion Integrated Rack on the ISS, using H2/CH4/diluent mixtures (soot-free) and C2H4/diluent mixtures (sooty) at different flow rates, with nitrogen, helium and carbon dioxide as diluents. Synchronized spectrally resolved images, flame and burner temperatures, radiative flux and operating conditions (reactant flow rates, ambient temperature, pressure, acceleration levels) were recorded. Objectives were the transient flame structure, convective/kinetic and radiative/kinetic extinction limits, and the onset and nature of pulsating instabilities, for comparison with detailed transient simulations.

pillar.reason: The investigation determines extinction limits and soot suppression limits of gas flames, which describe when a flame can be sustained. The record names no direct fire-safety application; its stated impacts are for combustion engines and fundamental science.

environments.reason: Tests were run aboard the International Space Station, so they describe gas-flame behavior and extinction in station microgravity. The record names no specific crew-atmosphere condition.
